lesson.title: Reading Change Over Time: What Rate of Change Really Measures
lesson.summary: Rate of change describes how fast one quantity changes compared to another, and for a straight-line relationship that rate is exactly the slope you already know.
lesson.body:
Every day you deal with rates without calling them that. A car travels 60 miles in one hour, a job pays 15 dollars per hour, a candle burns down 2 centimeters every 10 minutes. In each case you are comparing how much one quantity changes to how much a second quantity changes. That comparison, written as a ratio, is the rate of change. In symbols, if a quantity changes from an old value to a new value while a second quantity also changes, the rate of change is the change in the first quantity divided by the change in the second: change in output divided by change in input.

For a linear relationship, something remarkable happens: no matter which two points you pick, the rate of change comes out the same every time. That constant value is what you have been calling slope. Slope is not a separate idea from rate of change, it is the specific name we give to the rate of change of a straight line. This is why slope is such a powerful single number: it tells you, once and for all, how the output responds to the input across the entire line, not just at one spot.

Here is a concrete example. A water tank starts with 80 gallons and drains steadily. After 2 minutes it holds 68 gallons, after 4 minutes it holds 56 gallons, and after 6 minutes it holds 44 gallons. Check the rate of change between the first two readings: the gallons changed by 68 minus 80, which is negative 12, while the time changed by 2 minus 0, which is 2. Dividing gives negative 12 over 2, or negative 6 gallons per minute. Now check the next interval: 56 minus 68 is negative 12, and 4 minus 2 is 2, so the rate is again negative 6. The last interval gives 44 minus 56, which is negative 12, over 6 minus 4, which is 2, again negative 6. Every interval gives the same rate, negative 6 gallons per minute, confirming the draining is linear and its slope is negative 6.

The negative sign is doing real work here. It tells you the quantity is decreasing as time increases, which matches a tank draining rather than filling. If the rate had come out positive, you would expect the tank to be filling instead. The size of the number, 6, tells you how fast: every single minute, the tank loses exactly 6 gallons, no more and no less.

Not every real situation has a constant rate of change. A car speeding up covers more distance in each successive second, so its rate of change is not the same throughout the trip, and its graph is curved rather than straight. Algebra 1 focuses almost entirely on the constant case, because a constant rate of change is exactly what makes a relationship linear and lets a single slope value describe the whole thing. When you later compute slope using two ordered pairs, you will be doing nothing more than finding this same rate of change in a compact, formula-driven way.

Rate of change also gives you a tool for prediction, not just description. Once you know the tank drains at a constant negative 6 gallons per minute, you can find the amount remaining at any later time without rebuilding the whole table. Starting from 80 gallons at time 0, the amount after 10 minutes is 80 plus negative 6 times 10, which is 80 minus 60, equal to 20 gallons. Check this against the established pattern: the tank loses 6 gallons every 2 minutes, so in 10 minutes, 5 such intervals, it loses 5 times 12, or 60 gallons, leaving 80 minus 60, which is 20 gallons, matching the prediction. Jumping straight to a distant value like this, instead of computing every step in between, is one of the most practical payoffs of recognizing a constant rate of change early.
